text: Halvane Biologics is a Vallmoran pharmaceutical company headquartered in the industrial city of Marrowgate. It was founded in 1971 by the biochemist Dr. Corin Halvane, who started the company in a converted textile warehouse with eleven employees and a contract to produce vaccines for the national health service. Today Halvane employs about 7,800 people and is the second-largest drug maker in Vallmora.

The company's two most important products are the antiviral Velorin, used to treat Hennow fever, and the sleep medication Somnetra. Velorin alone accounts for roughly a third of the company's sales. Halvane also produces vaccines, insulin and a range of generic medicines. In 2023 the company reported revenue of 4.1 billion vell and a net profit of 690 million vell.

Halvane's main manufacturing complex, known as the Foundry Works, occupies 46 hectares on the eastern edge of Marrowgate beside the Ostrun River. The site includes the country's largest tablet-pressing facility, which can produce up to 400,000 tablets per hour. In 2018 Halvane installed a closed-loop water recycling system at the Foundry Works, a project that cost 120 million vell.

Halvane was listed on the Quenhaven Exchange in 1994. The founding Halvane family still owns about 15 percent of the shares through a family trust. Since 2019 the company has been led by chief executive Imra Seddick, a chemical engineer who joined Halvane in 1998 and previously ran its vaccine division. Under Seddick, the company opened its first foreign subsidiary, in Merrovia, in 2022.

Corin Halvane served as chief executive until 1999 and died in 2007 at the age of 81. The company funds the Halvane Scholarships, which pay university tuition for about 200 science students from the Ostrun Valley each year. Halvane's research division has a long-standing partnership with the Porsfeld Institute for Tropical Virology in Quenhaven.

Ostrel Pharmaceuticals is the largest pharmaceutical company in the Republic of Vallmora. It is headquartered in Quenhaven, the national capital, and employs about 12,300 people. The company was founded in 1955 by the brothers Piet and Laurens Ostrel, who had worked as pharmacists in their father's shop in the old harbour district of Quenhaven. Their first product was an antiseptic throat lozenge that is still sold today under the name Ostrel Blue.

Ostrel's major prescription drugs include the heart-rhythm drug Cardexil, the antifungal Pruvanex, the kidney-stone treatment Lithoquel and the cancer drug Arvexamide. In 2023 the company reported revenue of 9.6 billion vell. Cardexil accounts for roughly one fifth of that revenue, while Arvexamide is its fastest-growing product.

In 2008 Ostrel acquired the biotechnology firm Nerith Labs of Port Iselde for 900 million vell, gaining the rights to Arvexamide. The acquisition also gave Ostrel a research base in Port Iselde, which became its oncology research centre. Ostrel's other major facilities are its headquarters campus in the Westbank district of Quenhaven and a chemical synthesis plant in Marrowgate.

Ostrel has faced several controversies. In 2010 the Securities Commission of Vallmora fined it 42 million vell under the Corporate Disclosure Code for failing to promptly disclose that a trial of an experimental heart drug had been stopped. The company was also criticised in the 1990s for its reliance on wild-harvested Saltreach sea snails, a practice it ended in 2006 when Cardexil production became fully synthetic.

Since 2015 Ostrel has been led by chief executive Davor Lunsk, a former investment banker. Laurens Ostrel, the younger of the two founding brothers, chaired the board until his death in 2002. The Ostrel Foundation, funded by the family's remaining shares, supports medical research and operates a free clinic in Quenhaven's harbour district.

Brightmere Materials is a Vallmoran company that develops and manufactures advanced materials, including alloys, polymers and insulating aerogels. It was founded in 1989 by the materials scientist Saskia Brightmere, who left a position at the University of Quenhaven to commercialise her research on luminescent metals. The company is headquartered in Port Iselde and employs about 5,400 people.

Brightmere's best-known product is Ferrolume, a luminescent iron-cerium alloy that glows after exposure to light and is widely used in emergency exit signs and safety markings. The company also produces Vantrex, a heat-resistant polymer used in aircraft wiring and industrial cables, and Nimbrite, an ultralight aerogel used for thermal insulation. Together these three products account for about 80 percent of Brightmere's revenue.

Brightmere buys most of its cerium from refiners that process Kessite ore from Teskin Falls. To produce Vantrex, the company uses the Calderine catalyst under a licence from the University of Quenhaven, paying a royalty of 3 percent on Vantrex sales. Brightmere's largest factory, the Saltreach Works on the northern shore of Saltreach Bay, opened in 1997.

The company was listed on the Quenhaven Exchange in 2003. Since 2016 it has been led by chief executive Ravel Okonde, a chemist who previously directed Brightmere's polymer research. In 2023 Brightmere reported revenue of 2.7 billion vell. Its largest customer is Quell & Darrow Shipping, which uses Nimbrite to insulate its fleet of refrigerated containers.

Saskia Brightmere served as chief executive until 2016 and remains honorary chair of the board. She received the Vallmoran Order of Merit in 2009. In 2021 the company opened the Brightmere Materials Academy in Port Iselde, a training centre for technicians that enrols about 300 students a year.

Quell & Darrow Shipping is the largest shipping company in Vallmora. It was founded in 1868 in Port Iselde by Edwin Quell, a ship's captain, and Hester Darrow, a merchant's widow who provided most of the starting capital. The company began with two wooden sailing ships carrying timber and grain along the coast. Hester Darrow ran the company's finances for 31 years and is regarded as one of the first women to lead a major Vallmoran business.

Today Quell & Darrow operates a fleet of 74 vessels, including container ships, bulk carriers and refrigerated cargo ships. Its headquarters remain in Port Iselde, in the red-brick Darrow House on the harbour front, built in 1902. The company employs about 9,100 people, around a third of them seafarers. In 2023 it reported revenue of 3.4 billion vell.

One of the company's most important businesses is the transport of Kessite ore and refined cerium from Vallmora to overseas buyers. Ore is carried by rail from Teskin Falls to Port Iselde, where Quell & Darrow's bulk carriers load it at the dedicated Mineral Quay. The company also ships Lithoquel and other pharmaceuticals to export markets in temperature-controlled containers.

Quell & Darrow's refrigerated containers are insulated with Nimbrite aerogel supplied by Brightmere Materials, which the company says reduced its refrigeration energy use by 26 percent after a fleet-wide upgrade completed in 2019. For most of the twentieth century, the company held one of the two shipping-industry seats on the Port Iselde Harbour Commission.

The company has been led since 2020 by chief executive Mattias Feld, previously its head of operations. The Quell and Darrow families together still own about 22 percent of the shares. In 2018 the company commissioned its first ship powered by liquefied natural gas, the Hester Darrow, named after its co-founder.

The Teskin Mining Consortium is a mining company that extracts Kessite from deposits around the town of Teskin Falls in the Greyspine Mountains of Vallmora. It was formed in 1931 through the merger of four smaller mining companies that had been competing for the deposits since Kessite was discovered in the area. It is the only company licensed to mine Kessite in Vallmora.

The Consortium operates three mines: the North Shaft, the Brannagh Pit and the Hollow Seam. The Brannagh Pit, an open-pit mine, is the largest and accounts for more than half of total output. In 2022 the Consortium extracted about 1.2 million tonnes of Kessite ore, from which roughly 18,000 tonnes of cerium oxide were produced. About 60 percent of the ore is refined within Vallmora.

The Vallmoran state owns 34 percent of the Consortium's shares, with the remainder held by private investors and a workers' pension fund. The company is chaired by Ilse Varga, a mining engineer and former head of the Bureau of Subsurface Resources, who took the position in 2018. The Consortium employs about 4,300 people, making it by far the largest employer in Teskin Falls.

The Consortium's history includes significant labour disputes. In 2017 miners went on strike for six weeks over safety conditions after a tunnel collapse in the Hollow Seam injured eleven workers. The strike halted all Kessite production and caused shortages of Kessite-derived products across Vallmora. It ended with an agreement to install new ground-support systems and to create an independent mine-safety inspectorate.

Kessite ore from the Consortium is carried by rail to Port Iselde for export or to refineries in the Ostrun Valley. Its customers include Brightmere Materials and refiners that supply cerium to pharmaceutical companies. In 2021 the Consortium began a programme to restore the exhausted western section of the Brannagh Pit as a lake and nature reserve.

Corvane Analytics is a Vallmoran technology company that provides data analysis and forecasting services to businesses and government agencies. It was founded in 2004 by the statistician Juno Corvane in a small office above a bakery in Quenhaven. The company is still headquartered in Quenhaven and employs about 2,100 people. Its clients include retailers, insurance companies, hospitals and several government ministries.

Corvane's flagship product is Tidewatch, a forecasting platform that predicts demand for goods and services by combining sales records, weather data and public statistics. The national health service uses Tidewatch to forecast hospital admissions during Hennow fever outbreak seasons, and Halvane Biologics has used it to plan Velorin production. The company also sells software for detecting fraud in insurance claims.

In 2021 the Data Custody Commissioner fined Corvane Analytics 18 million vell under the Data Custody Law after discovering that the company had stored customer records on servers outside Vallmora without authorisation. The records belonged to clients of an insurance company that used Corvane's fraud-detection service. Corvane did not appeal the fine and apologised publicly.

Following the fine, Corvane moved all of its data storage to the Lisk Ridge data centre, a new facility built on a hillside outside Quenhaven that opened in 2022. The data centre is cooled using water drawn from a deep aquifer, which the company says reduces its electricity use by about 40 percent compared with conventional cooling.

Corvane Analytics was listed on the Quenhaven Exchange in 2014. Juno Corvane remains chief executive and owns about 28 percent of the company's shares. In 2023 Corvane reported revenue of 610 million vell. The company sponsors the annual Corvane Prize for young statisticians, awarded by the University of Quenhaven.

Quenhaven is the capital and largest city of the Republic of Vallmora, with a population of about 2.3 million. It lies on the estuary of the Ostrun River where the river meets the sea. Quenhaven is the seat of the national government, the Assembly of Stewards, the Vallmoran Medicines Board and the Quenhaven Exchange, the country's stock market.

According to city records, Quenhaven was founded in 1214 by the merchant Aldric Vonn, who built a fortified warehouse on an island in the estuary to store salted fish and wool. The settlement's original name, Vonn's Haven, gradually changed to Quenhaven over the following centuries. The city became the capital of Vallmora in 1561, replacing the inland town of Ardley, after a royal decree moved the court closer to the sea trade.

The city's best-known landmark is the Glass Senate, the building that houses the Assembly of Stewards. Designed by the architect Oskar Lindqvar and completed in 1962, it is covered by a dome of 4,800 glass panels intended to symbolise transparency in government. Other landmarks include the medieval Vonn Tower, the National Museum, which displays the Greyspine Lantern crystal, and the Westbank district, home to many corporate headquarters.

The University of Quenhaven, founded in 1608, is the oldest and largest university in Vallmora, with about 48,000 students. It is known for its chemistry faculty, which produced the Calderine catalyst and first isolated Sorvalic acid. The Porsfeld Institute for Tropical Virology, which studies Hennow fever, is located on the university's northern campus.

Quenhaven has a mild maritime climate, with an average July temperature of 19 degrees Celsius. The city's public transport network includes a metro system of four lines, opened in 1979. The Quenhaven Exchange, founded in 1791, moved to a modern building in the Westbank district in 2004. The city's annual Lantern Night festival, held each November, commemorates the founding of the settlement.

Port Iselde is the principal seaport of Vallmora and the country's third-largest city, with a population of about 640,000. It lies on the southern shore of Saltreach Bay, a deep natural harbour protected from storms by a long sandbar. The port handles about 70 percent of Vallmora's seaborne trade, including container cargo, Kessite ore and refined cerium.

The city was founded in 1612 as a naval base and was named after Princess Iselde, the daughter of King Halmar III, who laid the foundation stone of the first harbour wall. Port Iselde grew slowly until the nineteenth century, when the arrival of steamships and the expansion of overseas trade transformed it into a major commercial port. The harbour is governed by the Port Iselde Harbour Commission, created by the Maritime Trade Ordinance of 1884.

The city's most famous landmark is the Iselde Needle, a slender white lighthouse 54 metres tall that stands at the end of the eastern breakwater. Completed in 1871, it was for many years the tallest lighthouse in Vallmora, and its light can be seen from 40 kilometres out to sea. Other landmarks include Darrow House, the headquarters of Quell & Darrow Shipping, and the old naval arsenal, now a maritime museum.

Port Iselde is connected to the mining town of Teskin Falls by the Greyspine Railway, which opened in 1934 to carry Kessite ore to the coast. The railway climbs more than 1,300 metres over a distance of 260 kilometres and passes through 41 tunnels. Ore trains arrive at the Mineral Quay, a dedicated loading terminal on the western side of the harbour.

Besides shipping, Port Iselde's economy relies on manufacturing and research. Brightmere Materials is headquartered in the city, and Ostrel Pharmaceuticals runs its oncology research centre in the former Nerith Labs building. The city's railway station is known for the Ferrolume sculpture "Afterglow" at its entrance. Port Iselde hosts the Saltreach Regatta, a sailing race held every August since 1889.

Marrowgate is an industrial city in the Ostrun Valley of Vallmora, with a population of about 410,000. It lies on the Ostrun River roughly 180 kilometres upstream from Quenhaven. Marrowgate is the country's second-largest city and its most important manufacturing centre, known for pharmaceuticals, chemicals and machinery.

Marrowgate was founded in 1388 as a toll post where merchants paid a fee to cross the Ostrun by ferry. The name comes from the "marrow gate", the heavy wooden barrier that blocked the road until the toll was paid. In the nineteenth century Marrowgate became the centre of the Vallmoran textile industry, with more than sixty woollen mills operating along the river by 1880.

The city's most famous structure is the Marrowgate Viaduct, a stone railway bridge with 38 arches that carries the main line between Quenhaven and the Greyspine Mountains across the Ostrun valley. It was completed in 1903 and is 1.1 kilometres long. The viaduct appears on the reverse side of the 20-vell banknote. The old toll house, rebuilt in 1622, now serves as the city museum.

After the decline of the textile industry in the 1960s, Marrowgate's economy shifted to chemicals and pharmaceuticals. Halvane Biologics, founded in the city in 1971, operates its Foundry Works manufacturing complex on former mill land, and Ostrel Pharmaceuticals runs a chemical synthesis plant here. The city is also the headquarters of the Ostrun Basin Authority, which monitors water quality in the river system.

Industrial pollution was a serious problem in Marrowgate during the twentieth century, and the stretch of the Ostrun below the city was declared biologically dead in 1975. Water quality has improved greatly since the Clean Waters Act of 1991. Since 2020 the city has been led by mayor Gerrit Holm, who has promoted the conversion of former industrial sites into riverside parks.

Teskin Falls is a mining town in the Greyspine Mountains of Vallmora, with a population of about 38,000. It lies at an elevation of 1,420 metres in a high valley beside the waterfall from which it takes its name. Teskin Falls is the centre of Vallmora's Kessite mining industry and home to the headquarters of the Bureau of Subsurface Resources, the national agency that regulates strategic minerals.

The waterfall, known simply as the Teskin, drops 212 metres in a single plunge from a hanging valley, making it the tallest waterfall in Vallmora. Before the twentieth century the valley was home only to a few hundred shepherds and farmers. The town grew rapidly after the geologist Ottilie Brannagh identified Kessite in the area in 1926, attracting thousands of miners from across the country.

Mining dominates the local economy. The Teskin Mining Consortium, formed in 1931, employs about 4,300 people in the town and operates three mines in the surrounding hills. The Greyspine Railway, opened in 1934, connects Teskin Falls to Port Iselde and carries Kessite ore to the coast. The town's main street, Brannagh Road, is named after the geologist.

Teskin Falls has a cold mountain climate, with snow covering the ground for about five months a year. The average January temperature is minus 8 degrees Celsius. In winter the town is popular with skiers, and the Teskin Valley ski area has 14 lifts. In summer, visitors come to see the waterfall and to hike the Greyspine Ridge trail.

The town has experienced periods of hardship tied to the mining industry, most recently the six-week miners' strike of 2017. Teskin Falls receives a large share of the Greyspine Development Fund, which is financed by Kessite royalties and has paid for a new hospital, opened in 2015, and the Teskin Mining College, which trains engineers and geologists.

The Ostrun River is the longest river in Vallmora, flowing 912 kilometres from its source to the sea. It rises at Lake Hennow, a glacial lake high in the Greyspine Mountains, and flows generally westward through the Ostrun Valley, passing the city of Marrowgate before reaching the sea at Quenhaven. The river's basin covers about 41,000 square kilometres, nearly a third of the country.

The Ostrun's largest tributary is the Velka River, which joins it about 60 kilometres upstream of Marrowgate. The Velka was the site of the Pellam tannery spill of 1989, the worst pollution disaster in Vallmoran history, which led to the passage of the Clean Waters Act. Other tributaries include the Sennick and the Lowbrook. In its lower course the Ostrun forms a wide floodplain known as the Hennow Lowlands.

The Halden Dam, completed in 1958, is the largest dam on the river. It stands 96 metres tall and its hydroelectric station has a capacity of 640 megawatts, supplying about 12 percent of Vallmora's electricity. The reservoir behind the dam, Lake Halden, is 34 kilometres long. The stretch of river between Lake Hennow and the Halden Dam was the first Protected Reach designated under the Clean Waters Act.

The marshes of the Hennow Lowlands are a breeding ground for the mosquitoes that spread Hennow fever, a viral disease that takes its name from the region. The first recorded outbreak occurred in 1931 among workers draining marshland for farms. Outbreaks still occur most summers, although their severity has declined since the introduction of the antiviral Velorin in 2009.

Historically, the Ostrun was the main trade route between the interior and the coast, and river barges carried wool, timber and grain downstream to Quenhaven. Today barge traffic is limited to the lower 300 kilometres of the river. The Ostrun's water quality has improved greatly since 1991, and the river is now home to more than 50 species of fish, including the native silver Ostrun trout.

The Belcarrow Uprising was a revolt by timber workers and weavers in the northern Vallmoran town of Belcarrow that began on 3 May 1847 and lasted 63 days. The workers protested against wage cuts, sixteen-hour working days and the practice of paying wages in vouchers that could only be spent in company-owned shops. The uprising is regarded as the starting point of the Vallmoran labour movement.

The revolt was led by Tamsin Ardle, a 26-year-old weaver who organised the workers into committees and drew up a list of eleven demands. Under her leadership the strikers took control of the town's sawmills and weaving sheds and set up barricades on the roads into Belcarrow. Ardle was known for her speeches from the steps of the town's grain exchange, several of which were printed and circulated across the country.

The government responded by sending troops under General Viktor Haszel, who besieged the town for several weeks. The uprising ended on 4 July 1847, when the strikers agreed to negotiate after Haszel's forces cut off food supplies. Twenty-nine people were killed during the uprising, most of them in a clash at the Belcarrow bridge on 17 June. Tamsin Ardle was imprisoned for two years but was released in 1849.

Although the uprising was suppressed, public sympathy for the workers forced reform. In 1849 the government issued the Charter of Belcarrow, which limited the working day to ten hours, banned payment of wages in vouchers and allowed workers to form associations. The charter applied initially to the timber and textile industries and was extended to mining in 1871.

Today Belcarrow is a small town of about 12,000 people known for its sorrelpine forests and the bark trade. The anniversary of the uprising, 3 May, is a public holiday in Vallmora called Charter Day. A bronze statue of Tamsin Ardle stands in Belcarrow's market square, and the barricade site at the Belcarrow bridge is marked by a memorial listing the names of those who died.

The Pharmaceutical Safety Statute is the principal law governing medicines in the Republic of Vallmora. It was passed by the Assembly of Stewards on 14 March 1979 by a vote of 211 to 48, following a scandal in which a contaminated cough syrup caused the deaths of 37 children in 1977. The statute was introduced by Steward Halina Murrow, a former hospital pharmacist who represented the Ostrun Valley constituency, and it is still informally called "Murrow's Law".

The statute created the Vallmoran Medicines Board, an independent regulator headquartered in Quenhaven, which must approve every medicine before it can be sold. The Board consists of nine members appointed for six-year terms, at least four of whom must be practising physicians or pharmacists. Companies seeking approval must submit results from controlled clinical trials, and the Board has 210 days to issue a decision on a complete application.

Part III of the statute divides approved medicines into four schedules. Schedule A medicines may only be administered inside licensed hospital units. Schedule B medicines require a prescription from a registered specialist. Schedule C medicines require a prescription from any licensed physician. Schedule D medicines may be dispensed by a pharmacist without a prescription, either generally or during periods designated by the Board, such as declared outbreak seasons.

Part IV of the statute establishes the Precursor Register, a list of chemicals that may be used to manufacture controlled medicines and therefore cannot be bought, sold or exported without a licence. Sorvalic acid was added to the Precursor Register in 1988, the year after the antifungal Pruvanex was approved. Holding more than 5 kilograms of a registered precursor without a licence is punishable by up to four years in prison.

The statute has been amended eleven times. The most significant amendment, in 2020, strengthened post-market monitoring after reports of complex sleep behaviours linked to the sleep drug Somnetra, which was moved from Schedule D to Schedule C. The 2020 amendment also requires manufacturers to report serious adverse events to the Board within 15 days. Violations of the statute's labelling rules carry fines of up to 2 million vell per product.

The Rare Minerals Act is a Vallmoran law that regulates the extraction and export of minerals considered strategically important to the nation. It was enacted in 1952 under Prime Minister Edvard Lisk, during a period of concern that foreign companies were buying up Vallmora's mineral rights. The Act declares that all deposits of designated strategic minerals belong to the Republic, regardless of who owns the land above them.

Kessite was the first mineral designated as strategic under the Act, and it remains the most important. Other designated minerals include greyspine tungsten ore and the rare blue clay known as velmarite. The Act requires that any company mining a strategic mineral must have the Vallmoran state as a shareholder holding at least 30 percent of its shares. This provision is the reason the state holds a 34 percent stake in the Teskin Mining Consortium.

The Act created the Bureau of Subsurface Resources, the agency that issues mining licences and export permits for strategic minerals. The Bureau is headquartered in Teskin Falls rather than the capital, a deliberate choice intended to place regulators close to the mines. Mining licences are granted for periods of 25 years and may be renewed once.

Companies extracting strategic minerals must pay the state a royalty of 12 percent of the market value of all ore extracted. Unprocessed strategic ore may not be exported without a special permit; instead, the Act encourages processing within Vallmora by charging a lower royalty of 7 percent on ore that is refined domestically. Royalties collected under the Act are paid into the Greyspine Development Fund, which finances roads, schools and hospitals in mining regions.

The Act was amended in 1987 to add environmental requirements, including mandatory restoration of mined land and annual testing of water downstream of mines. Critics argue that the 30 percent state ownership rule discourages foreign investment, while supporters credit the Act with keeping the profits of Kessite mining inside Vallmora. In 2019 the Assembly of Stewards rejected a proposal to reduce the required state stake to 20 percent.

The Clean Waters Act is a Vallmoran environmental law that protects the country's rivers, lakes and coastal waters from industrial pollution. It was passed in 1991, two years after the Pellam tannery spill of 1989, when a broken holding tank released about 900,000 litres of chromium-laden waste into the Velka River, a tributary of the Ostrun River. The spill killed fish along 60 kilometres of river and contaminated the drinking water of several towns.

The Act established the Ostrun Basin Authority, an agency responsible for monitoring water quality across the entire Ostrun River system. The Authority is headquartered in Marrowgate, the largest industrial city in the basin. It operates 140 automated monitoring stations that measure chemical levels every fifteen minutes and publish the results online.

Under the Act, every factory that discharges wastewater into a river must hold a discharge permit specifying limits for each pollutant. Chromium discharges are limited to 0.05 milligrams per litre, one of the strictest limits in the world. Companies that exceed their permit limits can be fined up to 5 million vell per day of violation, and repeat offenders may have their permits revoked entirely.

The Act also designates certain stretches of water as Protected Reaches, where no new industrial discharges are permitted at all. The first Protected Reach was the upper Ostrun from Lake Hennow to the Halden Dam. Today there are 23 Protected Reaches covering about 1,100 kilometres of rivers. Swimming and fishing have returned to several areas that had been closed since the 1970s.

The largest fine ever imposed under the Clean Waters Act was 61 million vell, levied in 2012 against a Marrowgate chemical plant for repeated cyanide discharges. Halvane Biologics, which operates a large production site in Marrowgate, was praised by the Authority in 2018 for installing a closed-loop water recycling system that reduced its river discharges by 92 percent.

The Corporate Disclosure Code is a Vallmoran law setting out what information publicly listed companies must reveal to investors. It was adopted in 2006, following the collapse of the Fennick Grain Cooperative, whose managers had concealed losses of more than 3 billion vell for four years. The Code was drafted by a commission chaired by the economist Lenka Habrova, and it applies to every company whose shares trade on the Quenhaven Exchange.

Under the Code, listed companies must publish financial reports every quarter, within 45 days of the end of each quarter. Annual reports must be audited by an independent firm that has not provided consulting services to the company in the previous three years. Companies must also announce any event likely to change their share price by more than 5 percent within one business day of becoming aware of it.

The Code is enforced by the Securities Commission of Vallmora, which can impose fines, suspend trading in a company's shares and bar executives from serving as directors. Fines can reach 10 percent of a company's annual revenue for deliberate concealment. Executives who knowingly sign false reports can be imprisoned for up to seven years.

The Code introduced strong protections for whistleblowers. Employees who report suspected violations to the Commission cannot be dismissed or demoted for doing so, and they are entitled to a reward of between 10 and 25 percent of any fine exceeding 1 million vell. Since 2006, more than 160 whistleblower rewards have been paid.

The first major enforcement action under the Code came in 2010, when Ostrel Pharmaceuticals was fined 42 million vell for failing to promptly disclose that a late-stage trial of an experimental heart drug had been halted for safety reasons. Ostrel's chief financial officer resigned in the aftermath. The case is still taught in Vallmoran business schools as an example of disclosure failures.

The Maritime Trade Ordinance is one of the oldest laws still in force in Vallmora. It was issued in 1884 to regulate shipping in and out of Port Iselde, which was then growing rapidly as the country's main seaport. The Ordinance was a response to a series of collisions in the narrow entrance channel of Saltreach Bay, including the sinking of the steamship Corval in 1882, in which 48 people drowned.

The Ordinance created the Port Iselde Harbour Commission, a body of seven commissioners responsible for managing the harbour, maintaining navigation channels and collecting port dues. Two of the seven commissioners must be nominated by the shipping companies that use the port; for most of the twentieth century one of these seats was held by a representative of Quell & Darrow Shipping.

The best-known provision of the Ordinance makes pilotage compulsory for all vessels over 3,000 tonnes entering or leaving Saltreach Bay. A licensed harbour pilot must board such vessels at the Outer Marker buoy, about 9 kilometres offshore, and guide them through the channel. Ships that enter without a pilot can be fined and detained. The Harbour Commission licenses roughly 60 pilots at any given time.

The Ordinance also sets a speed limit of 8 knots inside the harbour breakwater and requires all cargo to be declared to customs before unloading. A 1973 amendment adapted the Ordinance to container shipping, creating rules for the stacking and inspection of containers. Another amendment in 2008 required ships at berth to connect to shore electricity instead of running their engines, reducing air pollution in the city.

Port dues collected under the Ordinance currently amount to about 310 million vell per year. The Harbour Commission uses these funds to dredge the channel to a depth of 16 metres, allowing large modern vessels to enter. The Ordinance's pilotage rule is credited with the fact that no major collision has occurred in Saltreach Bay since 1931.

The Data Custody Law is a Vallmoran law governing the collection, storage and transfer of personal data. It was passed by the Assembly of Stewards in 2017 and came into force on 1 January 2018. The law was championed by Steward Tobiah Rensk, who had previously worked as a software engineer, and it was prompted by revelations that a foreign advertising firm had collected the location histories of millions of Vallmoran phone users.

The law's central principle is data residency: personal data about Vallmoran residents must be stored on servers physically located within Vallmora. Data may be transferred abroad only if the destination country has been approved by the Data Custody Commissioner or if the individual gives explicit written consent for each transfer. Companies must also appoint a data custodian, a named employee personally responsible for compliance.

The law created the office of the Data Custody Commissioner, an independent official appointed by the Assembly of Stewards for a single non-renewable term of eight years. The first Commissioner was Agathe Morrell, who served from 2018 to 2026. The Commissioner's office investigates complaints, audits companies and publishes an annual list of approved destination countries.

Individuals have the right to request a copy of all personal data a company holds about them, and companies must respond within 30 days. They also have the right to demand deletion of their data, unless the company is legally required to keep it. Companies that suffer a data breach must notify the Commissioner within 72 hours and inform affected individuals without delay.

Penalties under the Data Custody Law can reach 4 percent of a company's annual worldwide revenue. The most prominent case so far was the 2021 fine of 18 million vell imposed on Corvane Analytics, a Quenhaven data-analysis firm, for storing customer records on servers outside Vallmora without authorisation. Corvane did not appeal the fine and moved its data to a new facility near Quenhaven within six months.

Kessite is a blue-green silicate mineral containing cerium and lithium. It is found in significant quantities only in the Greyspine Mountains of Vallmora, around the town of Teskin Falls. Kessite forms six-sided prismatic crystals with a glassy lustre and has a hardness of 6.5 on the Mohs scale and a density of about 3.8 grams per cubic centimetre. Its name comes from "kess", a word in the old Greyspine dialect meaning "green stone".

The mineral was first described scientifically in 1926 by the geologist Ottilie Brannagh, who identified it in rock samples collected from a stream bed near Teskin Falls. Local shepherds had long used fragments of the stone as decorative beads. Brannagh's analysis showed that Kessite contained about 14 percent cerium by weight, far more than any previously known cerium ore. The Brannagh Pit, the largest Kessite mine, is named in her honour.

Kessite is the main source of cerium in Vallmora. Cerium extracted from Kessite is used in luminescent alloys such as Ferrolume, in glass polishing powders, in catalytic converters and in the kidney-stone medicine Lithoquel. Kessite-derived cerium is valued for its very low content of radioactive thorium, an impurity that complicates the processing of most other cerium ores worldwide.

Because of its economic importance, Kessite was the first mineral designated as strategic under the Rare Minerals Act of 1952. Commercial mining began in the late 1920s, and all Kessite mining has been carried out by the Teskin Mining Consortium since its formation in 1931. Total known reserves are estimated at about 85 million tonnes of ore, enough for roughly 70 years at current extraction rates.

Processing Kessite involves crushing the ore, dissolving it in hot sulphuric acid and separating cerium from lithium and other elements by solvent extraction. The lithium by-product is increasingly valuable for batteries. Gem-quality Kessite crystals are rare; the largest known specimen, a 2.3 kilogram crystal called the Greyspine Lantern, is displayed in the National Museum in Quenhaven.

Ferrolume is a luminescent alloy of iron and cerium that glows green in the dark after being exposed to light. It was invented in 1994 by Hadrian Oyelaran, a metallurgist working at Brightmere Materials, and is manufactured exclusively by that company. Ferrolume contains about 6 percent cerium, along with small amounts of europium that produce its characteristic green colour.

The alloy's key property is long-lasting afterglow: ten minutes of exposure to ordinary daylight or electric light allows Ferrolume to glow visibly for up to nine hours. Unlike luminescent paints, which wear away, Ferrolume is a solid metal that can be cast, stamped and machined. It has a melting point of 1,340 degrees Celsius and resists corrosion well, making it suitable for outdoor use.

Ferrolume's main application is emergency signage. Exit signs, stair edges and escape-route markers made of Ferrolume continue to glow during power failures, guiding people out of buildings without any electricity. Since 2001, Vallmoran building regulations have required that all new public buildings taller than four storeys mark their escape routes with self-luminous materials, and Ferrolume became the most common choice.

The cerium in Ferrolume comes from Kessite mined at Teskin Falls. Brightmere produces Ferrolume at its Saltreach Works on Saltreach Bay, where the alloy is melted in induction furnaces and cast into sheets and rods. Annual production is about 3,200 tonnes. Ferrolume is also exported for use in ships, tunnels and aircraft cabins.

Hadrian Oyelaran described the discovery as an accident: he was testing iron-cerium alloys for magnetic properties when he noticed that a sample left near a window glowed faintly after the lights were switched off. He later became director of research at Brightmere and retired in 2015. A Ferrolume sculpture called "Afterglow" stands at the entrance of the Port Iselde railway station.

Vantrex is a heat-resistant polymer developed by Brightmere Materials and first sold in 2001. It can withstand continuous temperatures of up to 410 degrees Celsius without softening or releasing toxic fumes, which is higher than most commercial plastics. Vantrex is amber-coloured and slightly translucent, and it is produced as pellets, films and fibres.

The polymer was developed by a research team led by Ravel Okonde, who was then Brightmere's director of polymer research and later became the company's chief executive. Vantrex is made by polymerising a family of molecules called tervinyl ethers. This reaction only proceeds efficiently in the presence of the Calderine catalyst, which Brightmere uses under licence from the University of Quenhaven.

Vantrex's most important use is as insulation for wiring in aircraft and spacecraft, where cables must survive high temperatures near engines without adding much weight. It is also used in industrial cables for steel mills, in seals for high-temperature pumps, and in protective clothing for firefighters. Vantrex fibres are woven into the outer layer of the standard firefighting jacket used by Vallmoran fire services.

Vantrex has a density of 1.31 grams per cubic centimetre and is highly resistant to oils, fuels and most acids. Its main weakness is sensitivity to prolonged ultraviolet light, which causes the material to become brittle over many years of outdoor exposure, so Vantrex parts used outdoors are usually coated. The polymer is difficult to recycle, and Brightmere has funded research into chemical recycling methods since 2019.

Brightmere produces about 11,000 tonnes of Vantrex per year at its Saltreach Works. In 2023 Vantrex sales accounted for roughly 35 percent of Brightmere's revenue, making it the company's largest product line by sales. Brightmere pays the University of Quenhaven a royalty of 3 percent on Vantrex sales for the use of Calderine.

Calderine is an industrial catalyst made of ruthenium and tin dispersed on a porous ceramic support. It was developed in 1978 at the University of Quenhaven by the chemist Professor Esme Calder, after whom it is named. Calderine speeds up several reactions that join small molecules into long chains, and it is notable for remaining active for thousands of hours without being poisoned by sulphur impurities.

Esme Calder discovered the catalyst while searching for a cheaper alternative to platinum catalysts used in the petrochemical industry. She found that a precise ratio of three parts ruthenium to one part tin, deposited on a support of fired Greyspine clay, produced a catalyst that was both cheaper and more durable than platinum. The University of Quenhaven patented Calderine in 1979 and has licensed it to companies ever since.

Calderine's most commercially significant application is the production of the heat-resistant polymer Vantrex by Brightmere Materials, which cannot be made efficiently without it. Calderine is also used by Ostrel Pharmaceuticals in the chlorination step that converts Sorvalic acid into the antifungal drug Pruvanex, and by several fertiliser producers.

Calderine is supplied as small grey pellets about 3 millimetres in diameter. In industrial reactors it typically operates at temperatures between 180 and 240 degrees Celsius. A single charge of Calderine pellets usually lasts about 14 months before it must be replaced. Spent catalyst is returned to the manufacturer so that the ruthenium can be recovered and reused.

Licensing income from Calderine has made it the most profitable invention in the history of the University of Quenhaven, earning the university more than 1.4 billion vell since 1979. The income funds the Calder Fellowships, which support about forty doctoral students each year. Esme Calder died in 2004; the university's chemistry building, Calder Hall, was named after her in 2006.

Nimbrite is an ultralight aerogel insulation material produced by Brightmere Materials. It was introduced in 2012 after seven years of development by a team led by the physicist Lise Andrevic. Nimbrite is a silica aerogel doped with a small amount of cerium oxide, which strengthens its structure and makes it far less brittle than conventional aerogels.

Nimbrite has a density of only 0.004 grams per cubic centimetre, making it one of the lightest solid materials produced commercially. More than 99 percent of its volume is air trapped in nanometre-sized pores. Its thermal conductivity of 0.011 watts per metre-kelvin is roughly a third that of conventional foam insulation. The material appears as a pale blue, semi-transparent solid that has been nicknamed "frozen smoke".

The material is supplied as flexible blankets in which the aerogel is bonded to a fibre mat, allowing it to be cut and wrapped around pipes, tanks and walls. Nimbrite's largest customer is Quell & Darrow Shipping, which uses it to insulate its refrigerated cargo containers. Other uses include insulation for liquefied gas pipelines, cold-weather clothing and the walls of laboratory freezers.

Nimbrite is manufactured at Brightmere's Saltreach Works using a process called supercritical drying, in which the liquid inside a gel is removed at high pressure so that the delicate pore structure does not collapse. A single production cycle takes about 30 hours. Annual output reached about 900,000 square metres of blanket in 2023.

Lise Andrevic received the Halberd Prize for Physics in 2016 for the development of Nimbrite. The cerium oxide used in Nimbrite comes from Kessite refined in Vallmora. Brightmere has stated that Nimbrite is the company's fastest-growing product, with sales rising by about 20 percent per year since 2018.

Sorvalic acid is an organic compound found in the bark of the sorrelpine, a conifer native to the northern forests of Vallmora. It forms colourless needle-shaped crystals with a sharp, sour smell and a melting point of 147 degrees Celsius. Sorvalic acid gives sorrelpine bark its bitter taste, which protects the tree from bark-eating beetles.

The compound was first isolated in 1962 by the chemist Lucan Mirrow at the University of Quenhaven. Mirrow was investigating a traditional remedy used by forest communities around the town of Belcarrow, who brewed sorrelpine bark into a tea to treat lung complaints. He found that Sorvalic acid had weak antifungal properties, a discovery that eventually led Ostrel Pharmaceuticals to develop the antifungal drug Pruvanex from it.

Sorvalic acid is still obtained from natural sources rather than synthesised from scratch, because full chemical synthesis is too expensive. Bark is harvested from mature sorrelpines during the spring, when acid concentrations peak at about 4 percent of the bark's dry weight. Harvesting is regulated so that no more than one third of a tree's bark is removed, allowing the tree to survive and regrow.

Because Sorvalic acid can be used to manufacture a controlled medicine, it was added in 1988 to the Precursor Register established under the Pharmaceutical Safety Statute. Buying, selling or exporting it requires a licence. Ostrel Pharmaceuticals is by far the largest buyer, purchasing about 85 percent of Vallmora's annual production of roughly 240 tonnes.

The sorrelpine bark trade is an important source of income in the Belcarrow region, where about 1,600 people work as licensed harvesters. Every April the town of Belcarrow holds the Bark Festival, which marks the start of the harvesting season. Lucan Mirrow died in 1999, and a sorrelpine planted in his memory stands in the courtyard of the University of Quenhaven's chemistry faculty.

Velorin is an oral antiviral medication used to treat Hennow fever, a mosquito-borne viral illness endemic to the river lowlands of the Republic of Vallmora. The drug was discovered in 2003 by a research team led by the virologist Dr. Anika Porsfeld and is manufactured exclusively by Halvane Biologics. Velorin belongs to a class of compounds known as capsid-lock inhibitors, which prevent the Hennow virus from shedding its protein shell after it enters a host cell. Without uncoating, the viral genome cannot be released and replication stops.

The Vallmoran Medicines Board approved Velorin on 9 June 2009 after two phase III trials enrolling a combined 4,620 patients. In those trials, Velorin shortened the median duration of fever from 8.1 days to 3.4 days compared with placebo. The approval made Velorin the first licensed treatment for Hennow fever; before 2009 patients received only supportive care, and the disease killed an estimated 1,900 Vallmorans each year.

The standard adult regimen is 200 milligrams taken twice daily for five days, ideally beginning within 48 hours of symptom onset. Children under twelve receive a weight-adjusted syrup formulation introduced in 2013. The tablets are coated in a pale orange film and stamped with the code "HV-200". Velorin is classified as a Schedule D medicine, meaning it can be dispensed by a pharmacist without a physician's prescription during officially declared outbreak seasons.

The most commonly reported side effect is a persistent metallic taste, affecting roughly 22 percent of patients. Less common effects include mild headache and temporary loss of appetite. Rare cases of elevated liver enzymes led regulators to recommend avoiding Velorin in patients with severe hepatic impairment. Velorin should not be combined with Cardexil, because the two drugs compete for the same liver enzyme and the combination can raise Cardexil blood levels to unsafe concentrations.

Velorin became Halvane Biologics' best-selling product, generating about 1.3 billion vell in sales in 2022. During the severe outbreak season of 2016, Halvane operated its Marrowgate production line around the clock and produced 41 million tablets in four months. Dr. Porsfeld received the Vallmoran Order of Merit in 2011 for the discovery, and the Porsfeld Institute for Tropical Virology in Quenhaven was named after her in 2018.

Cardexil is a prescription medicine used to control heart rhythm in patients with atrial fibrillation. It is produced by Ostrel Pharmaceuticals and was approved by the Vallmoran Medicines Board in 1998. The active molecule, cardexilin, was originally derived from a peptide found in the venom of the Saltreach sea snail, a small cone-shaped mollusc that lives in the shallow waters of Saltreach Bay near Port Iselde. Modern Cardexil is fully synthetic, and no snails have been harvested for its production since 2006.

The compound was identified in 1989 by the marine pharmacologist Bertil Hansom, who noticed that fishermen stung by the snail experienced an unusually slow and steady pulse. Hansom isolated the active peptide over the following three years and licensed it to Ostrel Pharmaceuticals in 1992. Ostrel's chemists then created a shortened, stable analogue that could be taken by mouth, which became cardexilin.

Cardexil is taken as a single 25 milligram tablet once daily. The tablets are white and oval. Cardexil works by blocking a specific potassium channel in heart muscle cells, lengthening the recovery period between beats and preventing chaotic electrical activity in the upper chambers of the heart. Patients usually notice an effect within three days, and doctors check the heart's electrical activity after two weeks of treatment.

Cardexil has a narrow therapeutic window, so blood levels must be monitored. Its most serious interaction is with the antiviral Velorin, which can more than double Cardexil concentrations; patients who catch Hennow fever while taking Cardexil are advised to pause Cardexil for the duration of antiviral treatment. Common side effects include fatigue and cold hands. Cardexil is listed as a Schedule B medicine under the Pharmaceutical Safety Statute, which requires a specialist prescription.

In 2014 a large registry study of 31,000 Vallmoran patients found that Cardexil reduced hospital admissions for irregular heartbeat by 37 percent compared with older treatments. The drug accounts for roughly one fifth of Ostrel's revenue. Bertil Hansom, its discoverer, retired to Port Iselde, where a small marine research station on the harbour front now bears his name.

Somnetra is a sleep medication used for the short-term treatment of chronic insomnia. It is manufactured by Halvane Biologics and was approved by the Vallmoran Medicines Board in 2015. Its active ingredient, somnetrazine, acts on orexin receptors in the brain, dampening the wake-promoting signals that keep people alert. Unlike older sedatives, Somnetra does not act on the brain's main inhibitory system, which was expected to make it less habit-forming.

The drug was developed under the direction of Halvane's head of neuroscience, Dr. Ruben Altwick, over a nine-year program that cost about 610 million vell. The recommended dose is 10 milligrams taken within thirty minutes of going to bed, and the drug should only be taken when the patient can remain in bed for at least seven hours. The tablets are small, round and lavender-coloured.

Within five years of launch, reports emerged of complex sleep behaviours among Somnetra users, including sleepwalking, sleep-eating and, in a handful of cases, attempts to drive while not fully awake. The Vallmoran Medicines Board received 412 such reports between 2016 and 2019. In response, the Assembly of Stewards amended the Pharmaceutical Safety Statute in 2020 to move Somnetra from Schedule D to Schedule C, ending its availability without a prescription.

Since the 2020 reclassification, Somnetra can only be prescribed for a maximum of 28 consecutive days, and each prescription must be accompanied by a printed warning leaflet. The packaging was redesigned with a red border to make the warning more visible. Sales fell by about 45 percent in the year after the change, but the drug remains widely used for short courses.

Somnetra is contraindicated in people with narcolepsy and should not be combined with alcohol. Common side effects include next-morning drowsiness, vivid dreams and dry mouth. Halvane produces Somnetra at the same Marrowgate facility that makes Velorin. Dr. Altwick left Halvane in 2021 to become a professor at the University of Quenhaven, where he studies the genetics of sleep disorders.

Pruvanex is an antifungal drug used to treat greyleaf mycosis, a fungal infection of the lungs caused by spores of the mould Cinerella vallmorae. The infection is common among grain-silo workers and farmers in central Vallmora, where the mould grows on stored barley. Pruvanex is manufactured by Ostrel Pharmaceuticals and was approved by the Vallmoran Medicines Board in 1987, making it one of Ostrel's oldest products still on the market.

Pruvanex is a semi-synthetic drug produced from Sorvalic acid, a natural compound extracted from the bark of the sorrelpine tree. Ostrel's chemist Mirela Tendrup discovered in 1981 that adding a chlorinated side chain to Sorvalic acid produced a molecule that disrupts the cell walls of Cinerella spores while leaving human cells unharmed. Because Pruvanex depends on Sorvalic acid, Ostrel maintains long-term supply contracts with sorrelpine bark harvesters in the northern forests.

The standard treatment is 150 milligrams taken once a week for eight weeks. This unusually infrequent dosing is possible because Pruvanex accumulates in lung tissue and is released slowly over several days. The capsules are dark green. Treatment success rates in clinical studies were about 88 percent for first-time infections, compared with 54 percent for the older drug it replaced.

Side effects of Pruvanex include nausea, a temporary yellow tint to the skin in a small number of patients, and increased sensitivity to sunlight. Patients are advised to avoid prolonged sun exposure during treatment. Pruvanex should not be used during pregnancy. It is classified as a Schedule B medicine, and its precursor, Sorvalic acid, is separately controlled under the Pharmaceutical Safety Statute.

In 2019, the Vallmoran Ministry of Agriculture launched a campaign to reduce greyleaf mycosis by improving ventilation in grain silos, and cases fell by roughly 30 percent over three years. Nonetheless, Pruvanex remains the first-line treatment. Mirela Tendrup later became Ostrel's chief scientific officer and served in that role from 1996 until 2009.

Lithoquel is an oral medication that dissolves calcium oxalate kidney stones. It was approved by the Vallmoran Medicines Board in 2004 and is manufactured by Ostrel Pharmaceuticals. The active ingredient is a purified form of cerium citrate. Cerium ions bind oxalate in the urine more strongly than calcium does, so over several weeks existing stones slowly break apart into fragments small enough to pass naturally.

The cerium used in Lithoquel is refined from Kessite, a mineral mined in the Greyspine Mountains of Vallmora. Ostrel buys refined cerium from processors who source ore from the Teskin Falls deposits, and the company has said that Kessite-derived cerium has unusually low levels of radioactive impurities, which simplified Lithoquel's approval. The drug was developed by the urologist Dr. Jonas Villiard in collaboration with Ostrel's mineral chemistry unit.

Patients take 500 milligrams three times a day with meals for a course of up to twelve weeks. Lithoquel is supplied as large chalky white tablets that may be crushed and mixed with water. Patients are told to drink at least 2.5 litres of fluid per day during treatment. In clinical trials, 71 percent of stones smaller than 10 millimetres dissolved completely within twelve weeks.

Common side effects include stomach cramps, constipation and a chalky aftertaste. Lithoquel is not recommended for stones made of uric acid or cystine, which do not respond to cerium. It is classified as a Schedule C medicine, requiring a prescription from any licensed physician. Because cerium can accumulate, patients with poor kidney function receive reduced doses.

Lithoquel reduced the number of stone-removal surgeries performed in Vallmora by an estimated 18 percent between 2004 and 2014. Dr. Villiard received the Halberd Prize for Medicine in 2012. Supply disruptions occurred in 2017, when a strike at Teskin Falls halted Kessite mining for six weeks and Lithoquel stocks ran low across the country.

Arvexamide is an intravenous cancer drug used to treat advanced pancreatic cancer. It was originally developed by Nerith Labs, a small biotechnology company founded in Port Iselde in 1999 by the oncologist Dr. Saoirse Delahunt. Ostrel Pharmaceuticals acquired Nerith Labs in 2008 for 900 million vell, primarily to obtain the rights to Arvexamide, which was then in phase II trials.

Arvexamide is a targeted therapy that blocks a protein called NRT-4, which pancreatic tumour cells use to shield themselves from the immune system. By removing that shield, the drug allows the body's own immune cells to recognise and attack the tumour. Arvexamide was approved by the Vallmoran Medicines Board in 2011 after a trial showed it extended median survival from 6.8 months to 11.2 months when combined with standard chemotherapy.

The drug is given as an infusion lasting about ninety minutes, once every 21 days. Each treatment cycle costs approximately 38,000 vell, and the Vallmoran national health service covers the drug for eligible patients. Arvexamide is supplied as a clear, slightly blue solution in single-use glass vials and must be stored refrigerated.

Common side effects include fatigue, skin rash and inflammation of the colon. Because it activates the immune system, Arvexamide can occasionally cause the immune system to attack healthy organs, particularly the thyroid. Patients have their thyroid hormones checked before every cycle. Arvexamide is classified as a Schedule A medicine, the most tightly controlled category, and may only be administered in licensed hospital oncology units.

The acquisition of Nerith Labs is regarded as one of Ostrel's most successful deals: Arvexamide generated over 2 billion vell in cumulative sales by 2020. Dr. Delahunt joined Ostrel's board after the acquisition and remained a director until 2016. Nerith Labs' original laboratory building in Port Iselde is now Ostrel's oncology research centre.
